question: What goes wrong and what people believe that is false: why a vacuum fails to advance relfrozenxid, what cancels or blocks vacuum, MultiXact exhaustion, tables autovacuum cannot process, advice that newer releases changed (for example the recovery procedure), and common misconceptions about what VACUUM, VACUUM FULL and freezing do. Must find: each failure with its cause and the release it applies to.

sources.rank_basis: tier B: class (official post-mortem on the company's own blog, signed by its CTO; the role is shown on the page itself, lines 87-89)
tier B: class (vendor engineering blog, Percona); the reader comments on the page are community text
tier B: class (official post-mortem on the company's own engineering blog)

facts.summary: Metronome had four separate outages between 10 and 17 May 2025, each over an hour, in which write operations failed.
facts.quote: Between May 10, 2025 and May 17, 2025, Metronome experienced four distinct outage events, each lasting over an hour, that severely impacted our ability to process write operations across our platform

facts.summary: The root cause was PostgreSQL's protection against MultiXact member space exhaustion: crossing the global member limit triggered emergency vacuums, and writes were locked out until those vacuums finished, which took hours on large tables.
facts.quote: The root cause was identified as PostgreSQL's protective mechanism against MultiXact member space exhaustion. … we crossed a previously unknown and difficult to monitor global limit on MultiXact members, triggering emergency vacuums. This led to PostgreSQL's defensive lockout of write operations until these vacuums could complete—a recovery process that takes several hours for our larger tables.

facts.summary: Their metrics showed MultiXact ID usage under 50% of the threshold while the separate member space limit was being hit, and the page says PostgreSQL exposes no metric for member space consumption.
facts.quote: Our metrics indicated we were far below the configured MultiXact ID threshold (less than 50% utilization), suggesting we had ample capacity remaining. However, PostgreSQL was actually hitting a different, related limit - the MultiXact member space capacity. … PostgreSQL does not expose metrics for member space consumption

facts.summary: The affected system was an AWS Aurora PostgreSQL cluster over 30 TB running version 13.18.
facts.quote: A majority of Metronome's online infrastructure depends on an AWS Aurora PostgreSQL cluster exceeding 30TB in size running version 13.18.

facts.summary: MultiXact IDs are 32-bit (about 4.2 billion), and the member space is a separate store with a hard limit of about 4 billion members in total across all MultiXacts.
facts.quote: MultiXact IDs: 32-bit identifiers (maximum ~4.2 billion) assigned to each unique group of locking transactions. … MultiXact Member Space: A separate data store that maintains the actual transaction IDs participating in each MultiXact. This space has a hard limit of approximately 4 billion total members across all MultiXacts.

loc.heading: PostgreSQL MultiXact IDs: Technical foundation and our misunderstanding

facts.summary: MultiXacts are immutable, so each extra locker creates a new MultiXact with all previous members; n share-lockers on one row give O(n) MultiXacts and O(n^2) members, for example 5 transactions give 4 MultiXacts with 14 members until vacuum cleans them up.
facts.quote: MultiXacts in PostgreSQL are immutable collections of transaction IDs (members). When a transaction locks a row already managed by a MultiXact, PostgreSQL must create a completely new MultiXact containing all previous members plus the new transaction … when n backends share lock a row we make O(n) multixacts and O(n^2) members. … For example, locking a row with 5 transactions creates 4 MultiXacts containing a total of 14 members until a vacuum can clean up the old MultiXacts that are now orphaned.

loc.heading: PostgreSQL MultiXact IDs: Technical foundation and our misunderstanding

facts.summary: Concurrent inserts that reference the same parent rows through foreign keys create MultiXacts on each referenced row.
facts.quote: Foreign keys compound this issue. When multiple transactions insert rows referencing the same parent rows, PostgreSQL creates MultiXacts for each referenced row.

loc.heading: PostgreSQL MultiXact IDs: Technical foundation and our misunderstanding

facts.summary: Vacuum can reclaim member space only in contiguous segments, so one long-running transaction holding an old MultiXact keeps newer unused member space from being reclaimed.
facts.quote: PostgreSQL's vacuum process can only reclaim member space in contiguous segments. Consequently, even a single long-running transaction holding an old MultiXact alive prevents the vacuum from reclaiming newer, unused member spaces.

loc.heading: PostgreSQL MultiXact IDs: Technical foundation and our misunderstanding

facts.summary: When member space runs out, transactions that would create a new MultiXact are aborted with the error text 'This command would create a multixact with %u members, but the remaining space is only enough for %u member', and an emergency vacuum starts.
facts.quote: If the contiguous member space becomes exhausted, PostgreSQL will abort transactions attempting to create new MultiXacts with the error: This command would create a multixact with %u members, but the remaining space is only enough for %u member(Postgres multixact.c). Additionally, PostgreSQL initiates an emergency vacuum process

loc.heading: PostgreSQL MultiXact IDs: Technical foundation and our misunderstanding

facts.summary: Emergency vacuums started at about 200 million MultiXact IDs although the configured threshold was 400 million, because the member space limit was being hit.
facts.quote: we were hitting the separate MultiXact member space limit rather than the MultiXact ID threshold, explaining why emergency vacuums triggered at around 200M MultiXact IDs despite our threshold being set at 400M.

facts.summary: A failover to the hot standby during the first outage restarted the running vacuum processes.
facts.quote: In an attempt to mitigate what is now extremely prolonged downtime, incident response team triggers failover to hot standby, unintentionally restarting vacuum processes.

facts.summary: Replacing the running vacuums with data-files-only (no index) vacuums finished much faster and became their runbook recovery step.
facts.quote: Incident response team identifies and implements an approach to replace in-flight vacuums with data files only vacuum, which complete much faster.

facts.summary: The post is dated 15 November 2024 and was reviewed and updated in August 2025.
facts.quote: by Shawn McCoy and Divya Sharma on 15 NOV 2024 … August 2025: This post was reviewed and updated for accuracy.

loc.heading: MultiXacts in PostgreSQL: usage, side effects, and monitoring

facts.summary: An insert into a child table takes SELECT ... FOR KEY SHARE on the referenced parent row, so concurrent inserts lock parent rows and those locks become MultiXacts.
facts.quote: PostgreSQL uses a SELECT…FOR KEY SHARE on the table referenced by the foreign key. This can be surprising, because you are inserting in to the streaming table, but the rows in the song table are locked, and under concurrent usage those locks are converted to MultiXacts.

facts.summary: Savepoints also produce MultiXacts when sub-transactions lock or modify the same row; every PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION clause creates a savepoint, and drivers such as the JDBC autosave option add savepoints automatically.
facts.quote: If you lock or modify the same row in these different sub-transactions, then the multixact mechanism comes in to play. … Each EXCEPTION clause that you write in your PL/pgSQL functions or procedures creates a savepoint internally. … The PostgreSQL JDBC driver’s autosave option is one example.

facts.summary: The error shown when MultiXact member space runs out is 'multixact "members" limit exceeded'.
facts.quote: ERROR: multixact "members" limit exceeded DETAIL: This command would create a multixact with X members, but the remaining space is only enough for 0 members.

facts.summary: Autovacuum starts a MultiXact anti-wraparound vacuum when MultiXact age reaches autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age (default 400 million, restart needed to change) or when MultiXact storage exceeds 10 GB.
facts.quote: The autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age parameter defaults to 400 million. Changing this static parameter requires an instance restart after modification. … Aggressive VACUUMs are invoked when the storage occupied by MultiXacts exceeds 10 GB.

facts.summary: The page describes VACUUM FULL as rewriting the table under an exclusive lock, and FREEZE as freezing tuples so XIDs and MXIDs can be reused.
facts.quote: FULL (re-writes the table and needs an exclusive lock), FREEZE (freezes tuples to release transaction IDs for re-use – for both XIDs and MXIDs).

facts.summary: A plain VACUUM releases only MultiXacts older than vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age, so in their demo it released nothing; VACUUM FREEZE releases all completed MultiXacts.
facts.quote: For MultiXacts, a standard VACUUM command will only release MultiXact IDs older than vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age and remove their corresponding files from the pg_multixact directories. However, running the VACUUM FREEZE command releases all MultiXact IDs that are completed … A normal VACUUM won’t release anything in this example because these transactions aren’t old enough to breach vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age.

facts.summary: On RDS for PostgreSQL the size of pg_multixact/members can be read with pg_ls_multixactdir() (rds_tools), available from 12.21, 13.17, 14.14, 15.8, 16.5 and all 17 minors.
facts.quote: The pg_ls_multixactdir() function is available for RDS PostgreSQL version 12.21+, 13.17+, 14.14+, 15.8+, 16.5+ and all minor version for 17.

facts.summary: Before PostgreSQL 17 each SLRU cache (MultiXact included) had a single buffer area that could bottleneck under concurrency; PostgreSQL 17 split it into banks.
facts.quote: Prior to PostgreSQL 17, this caching mechanism used a single buffer area for each type of data, which could create performance bottlenecks in high-concurrency scenarios. … PostgreSQL 17 introduces a significant improvement by implementing SLRU banks

facts.summary: The MultiXact cache parameters differ by version: multixact_offsets_cache_size and multixact_members_cache_size on Aurora up to 16, multixact_offset_buffers and multixact_member_buffers from version 17.
facts.quote: In Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible up to version 16 inclusive, you can increase the following parameters in your RDS parameter group: … multixact_offsets_cache_size to 128 … Starting version 17 of Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible and version 17 of RDS for PostgreSQL, you can increase the following parameters in your RDS parameter group: … multixact_offset_buffers to 128

facts.summary: Long-running transactions, including read-only ones, make vacuum keep the information they may need until they end, for both XIDs and MultiXacts.
facts.quote: Long-running transactions affect vacuum operations in two ways: … 2. For read-only transactions: Vacuum must retain its information until the transaction is closed. This retention requirement applies to both standard transaction IDs and MultiXacts.

facts.summary: As a quick fix the page suggests VACUUM (FREEZE, INDEX_CLEANUP FALSE), which skips the indexes.
facts.quote: Use the VACUUM (FREEZE, INDEX_CLEANUP FALSE) clause to perform a quick vacuum by skipping the indexes.

loc.heading: Perform VACUUM FREEZE on specific tables

facts.summary: The Percona post is dated 13 April 2022.
facts.quote: April 13, 2022

facts.summary: Percona states that wraparound happens when VACUUM cannot keep up and that the PostgreSQL service is then forced to shut down.
facts.quote: Transaction ID wraparound occurs when the VACUUM process cannot keep up with database activity and the PostgreSQL service is forced to shut down.

facts.summary: Listed causes of wraparound: autovacuum turned off, long-lived transactions, logical dumps on a streaming replica, many sessions holding locks over large parts of the cluster, and heavy DML that cancels autovacuum workers.
facts.quote: Transaction ID wraparound can be caused by a combination of one or more of the following circumstances: … Autovacuum is turned off. … Long-lived transactions. … Database logical dumps on a replica using streaming replication. … Many session connections with locks extending across large portions of the data cluster. … Intense DML operations forcing the cancellation of autovacuum worker processes.

facts.summary: Percona gives 2 billion as the limit before a forced shutdown, countdown warnings from 10 million before it, and read-only mode at 1 million before it.
facts.quote: 2 billion transactions, or 231, is the upper limit that PostgreSQL permits before forcing a shutdown. … 10 million transactions before the upper limit is reached, warning messages consisting of a countdown will be logged. … 1 million transactions before the upper limit is reached, PostgreSQL goes into read-only mode.

facts.summary: Warning signs: many cancelled autovacuum workers in the log, and autovacuum running only to prevent wraparound, which is normal but should not be all it does.
facts.quote: Review the Postgres logs and look for an overabundance of canceled autovacuum worker processes. … look for a query string containing PREVENTING TRANSACTION ID WRAPAROUND. This is actually a normal message, but you should not see autovacuum running solely for the purpose of mitigating wraparound.

facts.summary: The warning quoted for fewer than 10 million remaining transactions carries the hint to run a database-wide VACUUM to avoid a database shutdown.
facts.quote: WARNING: database "mydb" must be vacuumed within 177009986 transactions HINT: To avoid a database shutdown, execute a database-wide VACUUM in "mydb".

facts.summary: When wraparound is near, the whole cluster must be vacuumed before fewer than 1 million transaction IDs remain.
facts.quote: You must vacuum the entire data cluster before the remaining available transaction ID drops to 1 million transactions.

loc.heading: Immediate Action: Approaching Wraparound at < 10 Million Transactions

facts.summary: Percona advises running vacuumdb in reverse alphabetical order to avoid the autovacuum workers and killing autovacuum workers that conflict with a manual vacuum.
facts.quote: Be prepared to execute vacuumdb against databases in reverse alphabetical order to avoid clashing with autovacuum worker processes, which vacuum in forward alphabetical order. … Kill active autovacuum workers when they conflict with a manual vacuum in order to speed things up.

facts.summary: Percona's recovery procedure after a wraparound shutdown is a cluster-wide VACUUM in single-user mode, using postgres --single.
facts.quote: One recovers from a forced shutdown due to transaction ID wraparound by performing a cluster-wide vacuum in single-user mode. … postgres --single -D "$PGDATA" postgres <<< 'VACUUM ANALYZE;'

loc.heading: Immediate Action: When PostgreSQL Has Shut Down Due to Transaction Wraparound

facts.summary: A reader reports that during a wraparound emergency all the oldest tables were TOAST tables, which autovacuum seemed to leave alone, and that vacuuming them directly worked.
facts.quote: When I looked at the list I realized they were all TOAST tables. Still trying to figure out why autovacuum was leaving those alone but there didn’t seem to be any problem manually vacuuming the TOAST directly and it progressed faster.

facts.summary: The post's author replies in the comments that vacuum cannot operate on a TOAST table alone, so the owning table must be vacuumed.
facts.quote: Because vacuum cannot operate on TOAST tables alone, as they are not relations, one has no choice but to vacuum the table itself that the toast is related.

facts.summary: The reader answers that autovacuum does process TOAST tables on their own, a manual VACUUM on a TOAST table works, and the TOAST table's relfrozenxid is kept separately from the main table's.
facts.quote: Autovacuum does process TOAST tables independently as seen in pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_progress_vacuum and I can run a manual vacuum on the TOAST table as mentioned earlier. pg_class.relfrozenxid of the main table and its associated entry for the TOAST appear to be maintained separately.

facts.summary: Sentry's post of 23 July 2015 describes an outage on Monday 20 July 2015 that lasted most of the US working day.
facts.quote: David Cramer - July 23, 2015 … On Monday, July 20th, Sentry was down for most of the US working day.

facts.summary: Sentry calls advice to turn autovacuum off, run it manually at quiet times or make it run less often awful advice.
facts.quote: The internet is full of awful advice from users suggesting you should turn off autovacuum, or run it manually at low traffic times, or simply adjust its schedule to run less often.

facts.summary: Sentry states that Postgres stops accepting commands when fewer than one million transactions remain before the maximum XID.
facts.quote: To protect you from this, Postgres will stop accepting commands when there are fewer than one million transactions left before the maximum XID value is reached.

facts.summary: Sentry reports the general advice of the time: stop the database and restart it in single-user mode to run the vacuum.
facts.quote: One piece of general advice is to stop the database and restart in single-user mode, thus running vacuum in a more isolated and safe environment.

facts.summary: Sentry chose to let the running autovacuums finish, fearing that a restart for more memory or for single-user mode would lengthen the downtime.
facts.quote: Our biggest fear would be that we’d restart, either to up the memory dedicated to the task or to switch to single-user mode, and we’d increase the duration of the downtime.

facts.summary: One autovacuum failed or did nothing visible, and the logs showed no failure because autovacuum logging was not verbose.
facts.quote: Unfortunately one of them either failed or simply didn’t work correctly. It’s unclear as to what happened, as the logs contain nothing to suggest failure and we didn’t have verbosity for autovacuums.

facts.summary: After the autovacuums finished, writes were still refused, because one very large relation had not been vacuumed.
facts.quote: autovacuums have finished, and the queue will survive (assuming we restore writes very shortly), but Postgres still isn’t accepting writes. … we identified that the autovacuums actually had finished on all of the relations except one. That relation however is a massive one.

facts.summary: Truncating that table restored service in five minutes, while a single-user-mode vacuum on a test machine was still running after 24 hours.
facts.quote: we made the call to truncate the table. Five minutes later, the system was fully restored. … we’re still watching one of our test machines run a vacuum in single-user mode going on 24 hours.

facts.summary: Sentry names its causes as too high an autovacuum_freeze_max_age, the default 3 autovacuum workers and too much vacuum cost delay.
facts.quote: We previously ran with too high a value for autovacuum_freeze_max_age and the default of 3 autovacuum workers. Additionally, we had been running with far too much delay in vacuuming

facts.summary: Their new settings included autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 500000000, autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0 and vacuum_freeze_min_age = 10000000.
facts.quote: autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 500000000 … autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0 … vacuum_freeze_min_age = 10000000

facts.summary: Sentry's update says maintenance_work_mem had a hard internal limit of 1 GB for vacuum, so the much larger setting was not used.
facts.quote: maintenance_work_mem has a hard internal limit of 1GB for the relevant paths, and thus our 100GB of memory dedicated to it wasn’t even being used.

conflicts.topic: what PostgreSQL does at the XID wraparound limit: shut down, go read-only, or refuse commands
conflicts.note: Percona says the service is forced to shut down (and goes read-only at 1 million); Sentry says it stops accepting commands at 1 million while still serving reads

conflicts.topic: can a TOAST table be vacuumed, and does autovacuum process it, on its own?
conflicts.note: the post's author says vacuum cannot operate on a TOAST table alone; a reader says both autovacuum and manual VACUUM do, with a separate relfrozenxid

conflicts.topic: recovery from wraparound protection: single-user mode or not
conflicts.note: Percona (2022) prescribes a cluster-wide vacuum in single-user mode; Sentry (2015) cites it as general advice but avoided it, recovered in normal mode by truncating, and saw a single-user vacuum run 24 hours; neither names a release

conflicts.topic: can MultiXact member space usage be observed?
conflicts.note: Metronome (Aurora 13.18) says PostgreSQL exposes no member-space metric; AWS names RDS/Aurora functions that report pg_multixact/members size, from listed minor versions

AWS states two triggers, 400 million MultiXact age or storage over 10 GB; Metronome saw emergency vacuums at about 200 million and ties them to the member space limit without naming a storage threshold
